item.title: Brazil’s Most Divided Town Shows the Nation’s Shift to the Right
item.description:
It felt like doomsday for the Brazilian left. On Oct. 4, Flávio Bolsonaro, the right-wing presidential candidate, outperformed polls and edged ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, a leftist.

The narrow margin was not enough to avoid a runoff on Sunday between the two candidates, but it was plenty to set off hand-wringing and soul-searching across progressive bubbles in big cities like São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro, and a reorganization in Mr. Lula’s campaign.

A visit to Nanuque, a cattle-raising, churchgoing town 500 miles north of Rio de Janeiro, where crowds turn out on foot for an annual march for Jesus and on horseback for the nation’s independence day, offers clues to Mr. Lula’s lackluster showing and Mr. Bolsonaro’s rise.

The town of 35,000 sits in the bellwether state of Minas Gerais, which has backed the winner in every presidential election since 1988, when democracy returned to Brazil after a military dictatorship.

Atlantic

Ocean

Amazon R.

BRAZIL

MINAS GERAIS

BOLIVIA

Nanuque

São Paulo

Rio de Janeiro

ARGENTINA

500 miles

The New York Times

In the 2022 race, Nanuque, pronounced nah-NEW-key, was the most closely divided of Brazil’s 5,569 municipalities, with Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, Jair Bolsonaro, winning by one vote. (Jair Bolsonaro lost that election to Mr. Lula and was convicted of plotting a coup after trying to hold onto power.)

In 2026’s first round, the younger Bolsonaro finished ahead by two percentage points, the same margin he claimed in Brazil as a whole.

Mr. Bolsonaro’s ability to win similar towns — rooted in agriculture and with a strong Evangelical Christian presence — contributed to his strong first round showing.

He won 79 percent of towns with a large agricultural sector, a high percentage of evangelical Christians and that have less than 50,000 residents, according to an analysis by Marco Faganello, a political data scientist at Fundação Getulio Vargas, a Brazilian university. Jair Bolsonaro won 53 percent of such towns in 2022’s first round.

In interviews with scores of voters in Nanuque, including truck drivers, cattle ranchers, farmworkers, business leaders and civil servants, those who have abandoned Mr. Lula cited unfulfilled economic promises, his past corruption scandals and their frustration with health care, among other reasons.

While many on the left remain staunch supporters of Mr. Lula, others who had voted for him before expressed fatigue over an 80-year-old incumbent running for a fourth term. His Workers’ Party has been in power for 18 of the last 24 years.

Valdirene Santos Moura, a cook who has voted for Mr. Lula before, acknowledged his accomplishments, including introducing programs that helped the poor. But now, she said, she was “tired of him already.”

Geremias Alves de Souza, a coffee picker, dropped his voice so his wife would not hear him say he was voting for Mr. Bolsonaro. He said he associates the younger Mr. Bolsonaro with his father’s tough on crime policies.

Other voters said their support for Mr. Bolsonaro was based not on his track record — which they said they were unfamiliar with — but on their affection for Jair Bolsonaro.

Some said they were simply fed up with politics and were planning to abstain on Sunday.

One is Jovenildo Carvalho, 45, who runs a start-up that uses drones to deploy wasps to attack caterpillars that ravage sugar cane fields.

Mr. Carvalho, who grew up with no electricity and wore Che Guevara T-shirts in college, said he has no faith in either candidate’s ability to lead the country, and was frustrated by Brazil’s deeply polarized political landscape.

“I’d like to see Brazil without the veil of fanaticism and blind passion that it has today,” he said.

Agribusiness in Brazil, which includes farming, cattle ranching, meatpacking plants and ethanol distilleries, has become a behemoth, accounting for a quarter of the country’s economy. For the first time, Brazil may soon surpass the United States in agricultural exports.

The sector’s leaders are among Mr. Lula’s biggest detractors, criticizing him over high interest rates, environmental regulations and gas subsidies that have reduced ethanol demand during the Iran war.

“If it were Lula against a stray dog, everyone would vote for the stray dog,” said Luiz Daniel Silva Rocha, whose family owns DASA, a large sugar mill and ethanol distillery outside Nanuque that employs hundreds of people.

The biggest target for local business leaders is Mr. Lula’s signature welfare program, known as Bolsa Família, which provides cash transfers to low income families. Brazilians agree that it has helped pull millions out of extreme poverty, but some now consider it a handout to those who aren’t financially desperate.

“In Brazil today, the policy is to reward those who don’t work,” said Ângelo Márcio Sousa Silva, DASA’s general manager.

Nearly 3,000 families in Nanuque receive cash transfers, according to government data, and business leaders say it has made it hard for them to fill jobs. Between DASA and the town’s largest employer, a meatpacking plant, there are about 120 full-time vacancies, leaving the plants operating below capacity.

The Bolsa Família program came up repeatedly as a driving force behind people’s votes for both candidates, far more than topics that dominate election talk among urban elites, like a scandal roiling Brazil’s Supreme Court or worries about U.S. interference in Latin American elections.

People who work in the informal sector — as day laborers on farms or cleaning houses — but still receive cash benefits remain loyal to Mr. Lula.

Letícia Silva de Almeida, 33, is among those. She works seasonally helping harvest coffee and earns $24 per day. She also receives $150 a month through the cash transfer program, even though she said that money was not essential.

“If they cut it off today, I’d be OK,” she said.

That mind-set infuriates others. Tatiane Souza da Silva, a housekeeper, said friends urged her to understate her income to qualify for the cash program, but she has refused on principle.

“I see young women in good health — men too — refusing to work,” she said. “That ends up hurting the economy.” Once a Lula voter, she plans to vote for Mr. Bolsonaro on Sunday.

Mr. Lula has called Brazil’s free public health system “one of the masterpieces of health care worldwide.’’

That is not a word many in Nanuque would use. Many complained of long waits for specialists in faraway cities, even though a year ago, Mr. Lula launched a program meant to help underserved towns called “Now There Are Specialists.”

“We need the politicians to see us, when it comes to health care,” said Ana Paula Rodrigues dos Santos, 41, who was shopping for the lunches she cooks and sells for $6 each to make a living.

She said she needs her gall bladder removed but explained that the town’s public hospital lacks an intensive care unit, which her doctors have told her she may need since her obesity increases the risk of complications.

She has been on a waiting list at a hospital in a city three hours away for nearly three years, she said.

Ms. dos Santos described herself as an independent who was leaning toward Mr. Bolsonaro.

“It’s been going left, left, left and the left didn’t do anything for Brazil,” she said. “We have to put in new people.”

The right’s increased appeal among voters is not just fueled by growing frustration with Mr. Lula. It is also driven by religion. The percentage of Brazil’s population that is evangelical Christian has tripled since 1991, and members of Evangelical congregations lean heavily conservative.

Dozens of Evangelical churches dot rich and poor neighborhoods in Nanuque, where some pastors preach opposition to abortion and homosexuality.

At New Life Evangelical Church, a relatively wealthy congregation, the pastor, Bishop Robson Merry Teixeira Farias, said he believed nearly all of his 300 members would support Mr. Bolsonaro for president.

Even within less well off congregations, support for Mr. Bolsonaro was still strong, according to pastors and members.

Under Brazilian law, religious leaders cannot make endorsements from the pulpit, but Bishop Merry, as he is known, suggested that preferences can be telegraphed by promoting conservative values that align with specific candidates.

“We do not champion men, we champion causes,” he said.

In a town with no mall or cinema, churches are central to social life, and congregants arrive well dressed and as eager to socialize as to pray.

On Sunday, after church services, they will have a second chance to socialize — at Nanuque’s 21 polling stations.

“As the election approaches, it is the responsibility of leaders” like him, Bishop Merry said, “to pass along their vision.”

“The sheep always try to imitate the pastor,” he added.

Silvia Ribeiro contributed reporting from Rio de Janeiro.

item.title: Why El Salvador’s Strongman Is Directing Threats at Haitian Gangs
item.description:
The skies above the slums and hills of Port-au-Prince are buzzing with helicopters.

Some of them are manned by a team of Salvadoran soldiers, medics and technicians who fly with machine guns at the ready in case they are fired upon.

The Salvadorans are deployed to Haiti as part of an international mission called the Gang Suppression Force aimed at eradicating rampant gang violence. Often tasked with evacuating the injured and transporting soldiers over gang territory, the Salvadorans once flew across the country to pick up a Sri Lankan soldier who had broken his legs.

The Salvadoran contingent in the U.N.-backed force is now the focal point of a high-stakes rescue operation after four of its members were ambushed on Sunday and went missing. Hundreds of Salvadoran special forces are expected to arrive in Haiti in the coming days, according to a person familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak publicly.

The episode marks a critical flashpoint in the Gang Suppression Force’s deployment, quickly escalating what critics worried was a slow, underwhelming start to the mission. With El Salvador’s president, Nayib Bukele, warning of a severe military response if his soldiers are not returned alive, the U.N.-backed mission threatens to become a showdown between Haiti’s armed groups and El Salvador’s contentious leader.

For the first time, the understaffed Gang Suppression Force, known as the G.S.F., is conducting operations in Croix-des-Bouquets, a town outside the capital where the Salvadorans were abducted that is one of the country’s most entrenched gang strongholds.

“I think this is a wake up call,” said Louis-Henri Mars, senior adviser of the Institute for Research and Action for Peace, a peace-building organization in Port-au-Prince, the capital. “Wake up call for the international community, for the U.S., for everybody: ‘Hey, we’ve been fooling around here, and those guys are not fooling around. Let’s get it on.’”

The New York Times spent three days last month with the international force, including with the Salvadoran helicopter unit. Troops from a Chadian contingent conducted patrols in armored personnel carriers. The commander of the international mission is from Mongolia.

But the force has been dogged by late deployments and logistics problems, which experts say have led gangs to meet the mission’s arrival with a collective shrug.

Haiti’s gangs control many parts of Port-au-Prince, forcing residents to flee some neighborhoods that have become no man’s lands. In others, gangs are so entrenched that even the police do not dare enter.

More than 22,000 people have been killed in a spiral of gang violence that worsened since the assassination of Haiti’s president five years ago — more than 5,000 so far this year alone. Gangs, once controlled by powerful elites and politicians, outgrew their overseers and banded together, taking over major roads and entire communities.

Touring a former school that the G.S.F. had cleared of gangs, Maj. Tahir Bahar, of Chad, acknowledged that his troops faced a steep learning curve: They’re used to deserts, not cramped urban terrain.

Expectations from Haitians are high, but he promised improvements.

“They want results,” Maj. Bahar said. “We must do it. I cannot promise a timeline.”

Haiti’s ability to hold cleared areas remains a critical obstacle for long-term results, including elections that had been scheduled for December that many here consider an extremely unrealistic goal. The school, in the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, is an area so dangerous that it still lacks residents and basic services.

“We need someone to come in after us,” Maj. Bahar said. “The civilians want to come back. They need electricity, and they need schools. We cannot bring electricity.”

The G.S.F. arrived in April with a mandate to take the fight to the gangs and take back control. Unlike a previous international initiative known as the Multinational Security Support mission, it would be five times larger, conduct intelligence-led operations, have arrest powers and work independently without having to coordinate with the Haitian National Police.

It is also funded by contributions to a dedicated U.N. trust fund. Expected to cost about $400 million a year, the fund has received $194 million, according to U.N. records.

The mission is supposed to have 5,500 soldiers, with contributions from countries around the world. Six months later, it only recently reached 2,000 troops, from six nations.

Troop contributions have been delayed, and moving people, vehicles and equipment across the world has proved a challenge.

The international force has cleared gang roadblocks, seized weapons and regularly conducts patrols in downtown Port-au-Prince, freeing up the Haitian National Police to respond to serious outbreaks of violence.

But of 26 arrests the force has made since its arrival, 18 people were released for lack of evidence. In one city, Gros-Morne, gangs killed civilians in retaliation for G.S.F. operations.

“We’ve got a long way to go, we totally recognize that,” Jack Christofides, the force’s special representative, said in an interview last month. “I don’t believe the gangs can sustain a fight against professional soldiers coming from so many different countries. We’ve got real capabilities coming — not just infantry, but police, we’ve got a maritime unit, we’ve got an air unit.”

The mission should have most of its forces on the ground by the end of this year and be making more progress by early next year, he said.

“We’re not saying that in two years’ time there will be no gangs in Haiti,” he said. “What we’re saying is that in two years’ time the Haitian state will no longer need an international force such as ours, because they can look after their own security and eventually stabilize the situation.”

From his social media posts, it does not appear that President Bukele plans to wait that long. In a message written in Creole directed to the Haitian gang members who abducted the four Salvadorans, he warned military operations would only get more intense.

“We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too,” he wrote.

Mr. Bukele, in office since 2019, is both praised and criticized for a harsh crack down on Salvadoran gangs that put tens of thousands of people in prison. El Salvador used to be one of the world’s most dangerous countries; now it’s among the safest.

The Salvadoran technicians went missing on Sunday after coming under attack while driving back from a supermarket through a gang-controlled area. Their vehicle was discovered burned, but the four Salvadorans have not been heard from since.

Although the attention is focused on finding them, the episode has raised serious questions about what they were doing driving through what is widely considered a “no-go” zone for foreigners and even most Haitians. While the incident is being treated as a kidnapping, many experts fear the men have been executed.

On Thursday, Lanmò Sanjou, a gang leader in the area where the Salvadorans were taken, released a video in which he refers to Mr. Bukele and shows buckets full of bullets.

“We will fight to stay alive,” he said.

Gédéon Jean, the director of the Center for Human Rights Analysis and Research in Port-au-Prince, said Haiti needed an international force to help shore up the local police, but that requires adequate technological and human resources.

“Unfortunately, this is still not the case, although the efforts are commendable,” Mr. Jean said. “We are still waiting for a full and complete deployment, and especially for tangible results.”

The ambush of the four Salvadorans will be a turning point for the international mission, he said.

“The disappearance of the four Salvadorans changes the situation,” he said, “because now it is the G.S.F. that is the victim of gang violence.”

André Paultre and Michael Anthony Adams contributed reporting.

]]>

item.title: North Korea’s Kim Jong-un Arrives in China, South Korea Says
item.description:
North Korea’s leader, Kim Jong-un, crossed a new bridge into China on Saturday in his first visit to the neighboring country in more than a year, according to a South Korean government source and South Korean media.

The reason for the reported trip was unclear, but it comes as Beijing and Pyongyang deepen economic and strategic ties despite heavy international sanctions against North Korea. This evolving partnership was highlighted by the opening of the New Yalu River Bridge, which is the largest border crossing connecting the two countries, earlier this month.

Sunday also marks 76 years since Mao Zedong sent his forces into North Korea to support the embattled communist forces during the Korean War against an American-led United Nations coalition. Beijing hopes to promote relations with North Korea to “new heights,” China’s ambassador to North Korea, Wang Yajun, said at a commemorative event this week, China’s flagship newspaper reported.

Mr. Kim arrived in the Chinese city of Dandong, a hub for travel and commerce with North Korea, via the new bridge, according to the South Korean source, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the diplomatic sensitivity of the matter. South Korean news media also reported the trip, similarly citing anonymous government officials.

Dandong features a large museum commemorating the military ties forged between the two nations during the war.

The trip was not immediately confirmed by Beijing or Pyongyang.

South Korea keeps a constant eye on the movements of Mr. Kim, and its officials have sometimes announced Mr. Kim’s past visits to China first.

A public appearance by Mr. Kim would help dispel recent social media rumors of his death, which South Korean intelligence officials had already dismissed as false.

When Mr. Kim has visited China in the past, he has held talks with its top leader, Xi Jinping. But if or when the two might meet this time was unclear. From Monday, Mr. Xi will preside over a four-day meeting of the Chinese Communist Party’s Central Committee, an assembly of around 300 senior officials, in Beijing.

Posts on Chinese social media showed traffic snarls in Dandong, and some said residential compounds in the city had been sealed off to prevent people leaving. The area around Wanda Plaza, a commercial hub in Dandong, was blocked, with neither vehicles nor pedestrians allowed to pass, according to other posts. One user of Douyin, a Chinese social media service, shared a picture of North Korean and Chinese flags along a road in what the user said was Dandong.

Yonhap, South Korea’s main news agency, shared its report that Mr. Kim was visiting China on Weibo, a Chinese social media platform, with no interference — at least not immediately — from Chinese censors.

There has been speculation among diplomats and analysts that Mr. Kim might attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, southern China, next month, though it is not clear if China has invited him.

President Trump, who has repeatedly expressed his eagerness to resume personal diplomacy with Mr. Kim, has said he will attend that meeting.

Mr. Kim is also trying to deepen ties with Russia. North Korea has provided Russia with critical artillery shells, missiles and troops for its war in Ukraine, prompting Moscow to sign a mutual defense treaty and supply the North with food, oil, and advanced military technology.

In response, Mr. Xi has moved to reassert Beijing’s influence. He invited both Mr. Kim and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to a military parade in Beijing last September. Rail service between Beijing and Pyongyang, suspended during the Covid pandemic, resumed in March, and Mr. Xi visited Pyongyang in June.

Bilateral trade has expanded rapidly. Decades of international sanctions have left North Korea reliant on China for nearly all of its external trade.

Mr. Kim’s first visit to China, and first trip abroad as North Korea’s leader was in 2018. Since then, Mr. Kim has traveled to China several times, holding talks with Mr. Xi each time. On his most recent visit last year, he attended a military parade in Beijing to mark 80 years since the end of World War II.

Murphy Zhao contributed reporting from Hong Kong.

item.title: Could Latin America’s Most Famous Leftist Be on the Brink of Defeat?
item.description:
No politician has made a bigger mark on Brazil than President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

Over three terms in office, he helped lift millions out of poverty, fought for workers’ rights and became, for a time, the face of a powerful leftist tide sweeping Latin America.

But the political currents have changed drastically and Mr. Lula, the region’s most influential statesman, is now facing a tough battle as he seeks another term. If he is defeated on Sunday, as polls suggest he might be, it would be the biggest win yet for the right-wing surge barreling through Latin America.

Right-wing candidates, aligned with President Trump on fighting drug gangs and waging culture wars, have won seven straight Latin American elections in the past 18 months.

As the region’s largest country, Brazil represents a major prize. A victory for Flávio Bolsonaro would tighten the right’s claim on Latin America, leaving Mexico the last big country controlled by the left.

Mr. Lula has offered a rare example of resistance to Washington’s strategy to project military and economic might in the region, pushing back against Mr. Trump as he has tried to squeeze Brazil with tariffs and sanctions.

By contrast, Mr. Lula’s right-wing opponent, Mr. Bolsonaro, has promised to join a U.S.-led regional security alliance and has offered Brazil’s vast critical mineral deposits as a way to lessen American reliance on China.

Mr. Lula, 80, is heading into Sunday’s race as the underdog, having drawn fewer voters than Mr. Bolsonaro in a first round of elections this month. Yet the margin between the two leading candidates was the smallest in Brazil’s history, with polls suggesting a narrowing race for the presidency.

In the final stretch of campaigning, Mr. Lula and his allies have worked to mobilize millions of Brazilians, on social media and on the streets.

Mr. Lula has also challenged Mr. Bolsonaro to open up his financial statements and phone records to public scrutiny, vowing to do the same. Mr. Bolsonaro has said he will oblige only after reviewing Mr. Lula’s records, which the leftist offered to electoral authorities this week.

What has become clear is that Mr. Bolsonaro’s promises to tackle organized crime, high grocery bills and a sluggish economy have resonated with millions of working-class Brazilians who in the past may have cast a ballot for Mr. Lula.

“It’s really about this profound sense of fatigue,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies the rise of the Brazilian right, said of Mr. Lula. “It’s the feeling that this leader, this project, has already run its course — alongside a deep desire for renewal.”

On the campaign trail, Mr. Lula has pointed to his economic achievements over the last four years, while also warning that restoring the Bolsonaro family to power poses a risk to Brazil’s democracy. Mr. Bolsonaro’s father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year-sentence for attempting a coup after losing the last election to Mr. Lula.

Mr. Lula has also defended his broader political legacy, built on decades of social programs that relieved widespread hunger, expanded education opportunities and reduced deep inequality in the last nation in the Americas to abolish slavery.

“Inequality and underdevelopment are the result of policy choices,” Mr. Lula told the United Nations General Assembly in September. “It is possible to include the poor in the budget and make the rich pay their fair share.”

Yet the leftist leader, whom former President Barack Obama once called the “most popular politician on Earth,” has struggled to stir excitement among Brazilian voters whose electoral priorities appear to have shifted.

Even though in the past four years Brazil’s economy has grown modestly and unemployment has fallen to its lowest rates on record, rising household debt and an affordability crisis have left many ordinary Brazilians feeling worse off.

Some of Mr. Bolsonaro’s libertarian ideas, like a hands-off state, lower taxes and cutting red tape for the self-employed, have also appealed to a growing portion of the working class that is migrating to the gig economy.

“There is a new kind of working class in Brazil,” said Rosana Pinheiro-Machado, a professor at University College Dublin who studies Brazil’s populist movements. “And it has a new way of viewing prosperity.”

If Mr. Lula is to secure a victory on Sunday, he will have to win over some of the millions of Brazilians who in the first round stayed home, voted for other losing candidates or annulled their ballots.

In an effort to lift his approval rating heading into the elections, Mr. Lula has increased how much people receive under the government’s signature welfare program and granted temporary fuel subsidies to ease the pain of rising prices because of the war in Iran.

He also expanded a government program to relieve indebted Brazilians facing billions of dollars in consumer loans. And just days before the first round of voting, he banned online betting, which has accelerated Brazil’s spiraling personal debt crisis.

This is not the first time Mr. Lula faces an uphill climb. Less than a decade ago, he was sitting in a prison cell, serving a 12-year sentence over a corruption scandal that appeared to have ended his political career.

But his convictions were annulled by the Supreme Court in 2021 amid evidence that the judge, prosecutors and the police had colluded to put him behind bars. This freed Mr. Lula to run against the elder Mr. Bolsonaro in 2022, a race he won in a huge political comeback.

Mr. Lula emerged on the political stage in the 1970s, making his name as a union leader on the outskirts of São Paulo. As president between 2003 and 2010, Mr. Lula, a former metalworker with a fifth-grade education, created generous social programs that helped some 20 million Brazilians climb out of poverty.

On the world stage, he has elevated Brazil to a leader on issues such as poverty, hunger and climate change, in part through his efforts to protect the Amazon rainforest. A skilled diplomat, Mr. Lula has also cemented Brazil’s reputation abroad as an important emerging power in the Global South.

When he left office in 2010, Mr. Lula’s approval ratings topped 80 percent. But the scandal that landed him in prison tarnished his reputation with a large slice of Brazil’s population, who still link him and his political party to corruption. Even after returning to the presidency, Mr. Lula has struggled to regain the trust of many voters.

Now, a new corruption scandal embroiling much of Brazil’s political and judicial elite, including Mr. Bolsonaro himself, is adding to the fatigue many Brazilians feel toward their political leaders. With the crisis unfolding on Mr. Lula’s watch, it has further dampened enthusiasm around his candidacy.

Ultimately, Brazilians will have to decide whether they still share his vision for Brazil’s future.

And, even if Mr. Lula is able to secure another victory, he will face the daunting task of governing a bitterly divided nation and navigating a legislative branch that has swung sharply to the right.

“Even if President Lula wins,” said Ms. Rocha, the political scientist, “it still marks, in a sense, the decline of a certain kind of leftism, of his Workers’ Party, and of Lula himself.”

item.title: Looting Left Damage and Fear on Paradise Street in Marseille
item.description:
For more than a century, Rue Paradis through downtown Marseille has catered to affluent shoppers, from the Mediterranean merchants of yore to those seeking designer fashions today.

Now, the avenue, whose name means Paradise Street, lies battered and in crisis.

Cracks snake across many shop windows, and others are boarded up. Some stores have been cleaned out by looters.

“Store is empty,” read a handwritten sign taped to the door of a perfumery. “Closed.”

A week ago, mostly peaceful demonstrations in cities across France devolved into clashes between protesters and the police. Then looters entered the fray, breaking into stores, supermarkets and shopping malls, and hauling off whatever they could.

In Marseille, France’s second-largest city, the pillaging hit the historic downtown hard, with about 500 businesses affected, according to the regional Chamber of Commerce. In one mall, Centre Bourse, looters sacked 32 out of 34 stores. Others set their sights on Paradise Street.

After days of government-imposed protest bans and curfews, a demonstration was expected to go ahead in Marseille on Saturday. As the day approached, merchants were still recovering from the looting while wondering why the police had been so unprepared to stop it.

“We never expected that we would live that,” said Nicole Richard-Verspieren, who heads a local business association. “There was fear. After that there was anger. Now people want to protect themselves.”

She spoke while packing much of the inventory of her wine shop into boxes to be moved elsewhere, just in case.

Other nearby businesspeople were installing security systems or nailing boards over shattered vitrines. Some were considering arming themselves, Ms. Richard-Verspieren said, adding that her association discouraged it.

Social conditions in Marseille, a city of 895,000 people on the Mediterranean, exacerbated the unrest, experts said. While it has an active cargo port, dynamic cultural life and significant tourism, it remains France’s most economically unequal metropolis.

“Marseille is a city that contains real poverty,” said Michel Peraldi, an anthropologist who has long studied the city. Many of its poor live in neighborhoods north of downtown that have benefited little from the city’s development. And a large share are young.

“That explains part of what happened, at least some of the frustrations that were expressed,” Mr. Peraldi said.

Paradise Street begins a few blocks from the city’s Old Port and heads south. Lining its downtown portion are quaint apartment buildings with wooden shutters, small balconies and ground-floor shops.

On the sidewalk, William Naim watched workers affixing boards over the front of his custom-jewelry store. He is a fifth-generation jeweler, he said, whose father left Tunisia for Marseille decades ago.

On the afternoon of the riot, Mr. Naim said, he received a notification that the alarm at his store had gone off, and rushed to the scene. Looters had torn open the metal grate over the entrance and broken in.

“They took all they could take,” he said. He, his father and brothers stood outside the shop until late that night to deter looters. One of them yanked off and stole his necklace, he said.

Like many merchants, Mr. Naim distinguished looters from protesters, whom he supported.

“The protests are important because we are in a country where we can express ourselves and where we can listen to others, whether we agree with them or not,” he said.

Down the street, a woman working for a gold dealer that had been ransacked said she had been shocked by her own children’s responses to the burglary.

Her son, 14, got excited when he saw looters breaking into stores, she said. Her daughter, 15, told her, “We’ll never have a chance to have clothes from Hermès.”

The woman, who spoke on condition that only her first name, Maha, be published, shared feelings common among protesters that the French state was failing its citizens. Her daughter is a good student, but worries that she will not enter a good university. When her son got injured recently, the family waited six hours for care at a state hospital.

“In France?” she said in disbelief.

Nearby blocks were a patchwork of shops that had been damaged and others that had been spared.

Stores housing well-known brands like Nespresso, Swatch and Longchamp were boarded over and closed. Dr. Martens and Intimissimi were also boarded up but remained open.

Outside a store whose sign read, “Hunting Weapons and Ammunition,” a man smoked furiously and declined to speak with journalists.

A nearby hairdresser, Kevin Varnier, 25, said he expected the security forces to act forcefully to prevent further unrest.

“The state can’t leave Marseille at the bottom,” he said. “The violence that was done needs to be paid back.”

To help local merchants, the Chamber of Commerce opened a drop-in center where businesspeople could report problems and seek aid.

Karine Guillem, an official overseeing the effort, said common concerns included how to protect their shops, make insurance claims, cover their rent and replenish their looted inventories.

Many merchants worried that the crisis was not over.

“The question that keeps coming back is, What next?” she said. “What will happen now?”

Sophie Boutière-Damahi contributed reporting.

item.title: Remains Found in Haiti During Hunt for Missing Salvadoran Soldiers
item.description:
Doctors examined burned remains found Saturday to determine if they were the bodies of four Salvadoran soldiers who disappeared after being deployed to Haiti on an international mission to crack down on gangs, according to four people close to the mission.

The remains were found six days after the men were ambushed while driving through a gang stronghold, said Scott Reece, a former State Department security official whose humanitarian aid organization retrieved them.

Mr. Reece’s group, Hero Client Rescue, a U.S.-funded medical evacuation service based in Haiti, said he was called to pick up the remains on Saturday afternoon.

The bodies had been badly burned and were not easily identifiable, three people familiar with the situation but not authorized to speak publicly confirmed.

But Nayib Bukele, the president of El Salvador, denied that the bodies were those of his nation’s missing soldiers. Just days ago, he had sent hundreds of special forces members to Haiti to try to recover the men, and had threatened to finish the gangs off if the men were not returned alive.

In a social media post Saturday night responding to a New York Times article on the discovery, Mr. Bukele confirmed that a nonprofit organization had delivered human remains at the airport, saying that they belonged to the four Salvadoran air technicians.

“However, the remains correspond to a child, a man of considerably greater height than that of our air technicians, and a person who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours. Among the remains, identification cards and military uniforms from other countries were also found.”

He posted identification of a soldier from Chad.

One person briefed on the situation said the identification Mr. Bukele posted belonged to a member of the Gang Suppression Force’s Chadian contingent, who was injured on the field and lost his ID.

The four Salvadorans had been deployed as part of a helicopter unit assigned to the Gang Suppression Force, a mission authorized a year ago by the U.N. Security Council to go after Haiti’s gangs.

The Salvadoran military said the men were driving through the Croix-des-Bouquets area near Port-au-Prince in an armored S.U.V. last Sunday when they came under fire and had to flee the vehicle, which was later found burned. The men were returning from a trip to a supermarket, driving through an area that is so dangerous that it is generally off-limits to foreigners.

They have not been heard from since, and no ransom demands have been made, people close to the case said.

The local news media reported that the Salvadorans were killed and then burned by Chen Mechan and 400 Mawozo, gangs that operate in that area, on the northern outskirts of the capital.

The missing men were aviation technicians who handled transport and medical evacuations for the Gang Suppression Force.

Gangs have wreaked havoc in Haiti for several years, taking over entire neighborhoods and killing thousands of people. More than 1.5 million people have had to flee their homes.

After another international police mission failed to quell the violence, the new anti-gang force arrived in Haiti in April. It has struggled to reach its full expected deployment of 5,500. It currently has just over 2,000 troops in Haiti, from Jamaica, Chad, Mongolia, El Salvador, Sri Lanka and Guatemala.

At least four G.S.F. soldiers have been injured in the search for the Salvadorans.

The G.S.F. declined to comment.

item.title: Iranians Face Anxious Wait as Threat of Attack Looms
item.description:
Many Iranians living in the country began the week on Saturday with anxiety and dread, closely following reports that the United States and Israel have drawn up plans for another wave of attacks on Iran in the coming days or weeks.

Parents agonized over whether to send their children to school or keep them close at home. Businessmen canceled work trips to avoid getting stranded if airports closed and roads became too risky. Residents in Tehran flocked to gas stations to fill up their tanks, withdrew cash from banks and stocked up on basic food items.

Some social media influencers warned their followers to keep a low profile in the coming days, and avoid unnecessary travel. Some people said that planning for war had become a new norm and they were feeling numb, as Iran has gone through two intense periods of fighting since June 2025.

“I just told my wife not to wake up our son in the morning, and keep him home, we can decide day by day how to proceed,” said Majid, a 42-year-old businessman in Tehran, in a telephone interview. He said his wife, who works at a ministry that could become a target, planned to call in sick. Majid, like all Iranians interviewed, asked that their last name not be published because of fear of retribution.

President Trump has said he was considering an attack on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections if a diplomatic deal was not reached, insisting that Iran could not have a nuclear program. American officials said last week that the United States and Israel have devised specific plans for renewed strikes.

Mr. Trump has swayed from threatening to annihilate the country to promising to rehabilitate its economy if they reach a deal. U.S. officials have said that the president could still veto the plans, as he has done in the past.

Iranians say his unpredictable nature only adds to their agony.

Shadi, a schoolteacher in Tehran, said she planned to show up for work every day unless the government closes the schools. “But in the back of my mind I keep thinking about how I can protect my students, how to act so they are not scared, if explosions happen during school hours.”

On Feb. 28, the United States struck an elementary school in the city of Minab, killing 156 children and teachers. American officials have ascribed the school strike to a targeting error caused by outdated data.

Behnam, a 38-year-old musician in Tehran, said that he felt numb and less afraid because he has survived two rounds of fighting. “What worries me and those around me most is the lack of money and simply surviving,” he said. “Everyone is trying to find a way to make money and get by.”

Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a tight election on Tuesday, said last week that the United States and Israel must join forces to topple Iran’s regime. The comments have raised concerns in Iran that Israel may carry out military strikes before the vote.

Negotiations have stalled between Tehran and Washington, despite a frenzy of diplomacy last week by Pakistan, Qatar and Russia. In public statements, Iranian officials have said they will not surrender to Mr. Trump’s demands about Iran’s nuclear program.

Iranians have seen their own government, from military commanders to lawmakers, make daily declarations about their intent to forcefully retaliate if attacked and set the region aflame. Hard-line supporters of the government, who are a minority of the population, hold nightly rallies chanting for escalation and revenge. U.S. officials said on Friday they had obtained intelligence that Iran was planning to target American personnel in the region.

Yet some prominent politicians and pundits have openly called for the government to tread carefully and do all it can to avoid a military escalation, fearing more suffering, destruction and instability for Iranians.

Javad Emam from the main reformist party addressed the government on social media last week: “The responsibility for today’s decision lies with you; the cost of war will be borne by the nation.”

At least 1,900 civilians were killed in 40 days of bombardment this year, according to Iran’s Red Crescent Society. The government said damages from the war amounted to about $300 billion. The economy has been in a tailspin: Sanctions and the U.S. naval blockade have contributed to the currency plunging against the dollar, and prices for some basic foods have skyrocketed more than 200 percent.

Alireza, a 54-year-old veteran of the Iran-Iraq war who lives in the city of Kerman, said that while he did not want Iran to surrender and suffer a humiliation, he was angry at the government’s lack of transparency and inability to find a peaceful solution.

“I hope the war ends as soon as possible, because war brings nothing but death and destruction,” he said in an interview from Kerman. “People are under enormous pressure and are being crushed by the economic siege.”

item.title: Speed of Starshield Satellite Network Is Improving, Ukraine Says
item.description:
Ukrainian drones connected to the Pentagon-funded Starshield satellite network have flown at speeds near 250 miles an hour for the first time since the system was throttled last week, Ukraine’s defense minister announced on Saturday. It was the first sign that the speed restrictions, which have hampered crucial drone operations, might be easing.

“This is another example when direct dialogue and the persistent position of the president of Ukraine at the highest level produce results,” Yevhen Khmara, the defense minister, said in a statement. “And this result is primarily important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics and communications.”

Ukraine uses Starshield for air defense and to guide drones toward targets in Russian-occupied territory. The unexplained throttling of the system deepened a growing rift that has been playing out publicly between Ukraine and the United States. President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Ukrainian civilians had been left more vulnerable to Russian attack, and Ukrainian officials raised fears that the Starshield program had been slowed to force Ukraine into capitulation.

Ukrainian drone operators first saw their drones slowed to speeds lower than 40 miles an hour about 10 days ago. Many drones slowed so abruptly that they lost connection to their pilots on the ground and then fell from the sky, wasting expensive equipment.

It remains unclear who, if anyone, ordered the system to be slowed. No one in Washington has taken responsibility, a fact that only caused further confusion in Kyiv.It has also deepened divides between Congress and the White House over the U.S. approach to Russia. A group of Republicans and Democrats in the Senate warned the White House this week that they would block President Trump’s nominations if Ukraine’s full Starshield capabilities were not restored.

item.title: Far, Far Away
item.description:
Kelly Green remembers the moment the world’s most remote inhabited island first came into view.

From a distance, Tristan da Cunha looked like a dark triangle on the horizon.

Up close, she saw the island’s tiny settlement spread below volcanic cliffs.

Then it became her home.

Supported by

Making a home on the world’s most remote inhabited island.

By Nick Schönfeld

Photographs by Julia Gunther

Nick Schönfeld and Julia Gunther spent 16 months reporting on island life during two trips to Tristan da Cunha between 2023 and 2026.

To reach Tristan, roughly halfway between Africa and South America, Kelly Green crossed 1,738 miles of the South Atlantic from Cape Town aboard the M.V. Edinburgh, a 205-foot lobster boat. She had never been to sea before, and she worried about seasickness, but it never came.

After a week at sea, the ship dropped anchor off Calshot Harbour, in front of Tristan da Cunha’s only settlement — Edinburgh of the Seven Seas. Its two small piers, jutting into the water, looked to Kelly like arms reaching out to welcome her.

Kelly could see most of the island’s residents (then 264 people) waving, including her mother and father, Marina and Sean Burns. Her father had been sent to the island, a British Overseas Territory, to serve as its administrator. He persuaded his reluctant 22-year-old daughter to visit, though Kelly, living in Britain, was more interested in clubs than remote islands. Kelly remembers him saying: “You have to come out, because you’ll never get the chance again.”

Among the men who helped carry her bags off the boat was Shane Green, 21. They met again that night at the island’s only pub. They danced.

Kelly went home after six weeks. The first night back in Cape Town, South Africa, where most ships leaving Tristan travel to, her hotel phone rang. It was Shane. They talked every night for months.

That was in 2012. Two years and several visits later, Kelly made the decision that would change her life: She moved to Tristan and became the first woman in over a century to settle there for good. The last had been three Irish sisters, in 1908.

Tristan was first sighted in 1506 by Tristão da Cunha, a Portuguese naval commander. Britain annexed the island in 1816 and set up a garrison for a year. A Scottish corporal stayed behind with his wife, their two children and two English stonemasons. That was the beginning of the community that lives there today.

Only 220 people now call it home, down from a peak of 300 in 1993. In the past three years, there have been 21 deaths and only six births. A few islanders have emigrated over the years.

Before settling on Tristan, Kelly’s life had been defined by travel. As a diplomat’s daughter, she had moved every few years — Antigua, Bangladesh, Senegal, Kenya — then became a flight attendant. Shane had never lived anywhere but Tristan. Where Kelly could describe the color of the sand on a beach in Mombasa, Shane knew every cove and gulch of his island and could explain, in great detail, the safest way from Green Hill to the beach called Down-Where-The-Minister-Landed-His-Things.

Part of what made it easier was that she and Shane, despite their very different lives, grew up watching the same British TV shows, which Kelly’s father had taped and brought to the island.

Living on an isolated island requires residents to be rather social — to pitch in for the common good, wear multiple hats, work long days and make their own fun.

Before Kelly moved in with Shane, he took her to dig potatoes, clean tripe and gut fish. He was impressed by how quickly she adapted. She said, “If I didn’t want to get my fingernails dirty, we wouldn’t have worked out.”

The couple married soon after and have a daughter, Savanna, 12, and a son, Seren, 5.

On Tristan, directions come in the form of “Up by Martha’s” or “Past Ricky’s.” Kelly and Shane’s home, which Shane built as an addition onto his grandparents’ cottage, sits at the top of the village.

When Kelly steps outside to hang laundry, she can see the vast expanse of the ocean stretch out before her. To her right lie the remnants of the 1961 volcanic eruption, a vast lava wall nearly 300 feet high that hems in Edinburgh, which residents call “the Settlement,” on its eastern side. Behind her, a giant cliff face closes off the sky above.

There is little of the ambient hum that fills most inhabited places — no traffic or electrical thrum. Even the diesel generators that power much of the Settlement are only audible up close. At times it is quiet enough to hear the rush of wind under an albatross’s wings, or the echo of a tumbling rock kicked loose by grazing sheep.

When winter storms hit, the only sounds are the roar of the wind and the window-rattling boom of waves exploding against the cliffs. Salt spray fills the air and eventually streaks everything with rust.

Most mornings, Kelly bakes bread and packs lunches before leaving by half past eight for her job as the island’s Head of Tourism.

At work, she might deal with a private yacht mooring offshore, sending her on a run of chores and errands — arranging tours, ferrying grateful guests to and from showers and washing their clothes. The next day might be spent fielding media questions, writing posts for the island’s social media accounts, or, on Wednesdays, serving lunch for a small group of expatriates.

Cruise season, from November to April, is her busiest time, when ships drop hundreds of ebullient and emotional passengers ashore if the harbor is calm enough to let them land. Some have waited years to visit. When a ship arrives, Kelly is down at the harbor, welcoming visitors with a clipboard and a walkie-talkie, making sure the islanders who’ve signed up as taxi drivers for the day, Shane among them, are ready, and the volcano walking tour sets off on time.

Shane works as a carpenter for the Public Works Department. He also fishes out of one of the bright orange lobster boats, the Verkenner, which he operates with his fishing partner, Steve Swain — part of the small fleet owned by the single company permitted to operate in Tristan’s waters.

On fishing days, Shane is at his boat before dawn with Steve, tying frozen bait to traps by the light of their headlamps. They’ll stay out all day and return around six in the evening, to find their daughters waiting with a cooler of homemade mutton pies and cans of soda.

Tristanian children have unusually free rein on the island. In summer, Savanna spends a lot of time at the community pool across the road from the pub, running around with school friends, or dancing in the same hall where Kelly and Shane first danced, and their parents before them.

Seren is more interested in helping his dad with the sheep and hammering nails into bits of wood with his friend Alfie. Seren and his sister both love the island’s black sand beaches, and ducking in to see their grandparents, whose doors, like most on Tristan, are always left unlocked.

One of the island’s few predictable moments of excitement is the arrival of a supply ship — they call about 10 times a year — bringing returning islanders, new cars, the odd visitor and the Christmas presents Kelly ordered months in advance. For a few precious days, Kelly can find Tristan’s supermarket shelves stocked with plums, grapes and heads of iceberg lettuce. She has to be quick, though, because the appearance of fresh produce triggers something like a doorbuster-sale.

The farthest Kelly and Shane travel regularly is to the Patches, a cluster of small stone-walled plots two and a half miles west of the Settlement, where Tristanians have grown potatoes, pumpkins and cabbages for more than a hundred years.

The family’s 24 “patches” sit inside a mosaic of low volcanic stone walls and wire fencing, built to keep the island’s cows out. Antarctic terns nest in the cracks of the walls and divebomb anyone who strays too close.

Shane is proud of his potatoes, varieties with names like White Blossoms, Smooth Skins and Americans. In a good year, the family digs up more than they know what to do with, the children sorting the harvest by size into old shopping baskets as their grandparents look on.

The couple uses their nearby camping hut, the closest thing to a summer cabin on the island, for a weekend getaway from the Settlement’s hustle and bustle. There is no internet and no electricity beyond a few solar bulbs. The ocean is just a few minutes’ walk away.

Leaving Tristan is difficult, and getting back is even harder. The two ships that call regularly carry just twelve berths each, with priority given to government officials and islanders needing medical treatment. Only the SA Agulhas II, a South African research vessel, which calls at Tristan once a year, has more spaces, but those fill up quickly too.

A vacation abroad is nearly impossible: Kelly’s family alone would take four of those spaces. The only other chance is a passing cruise ship, and those cabins cost more than most islanders can afford.

Kelly last left the island in 2023, for her father’s funeral. Sean had suffered a series of strokes while serving an unexpected third term as administrator on the island. No ship was close enough to reach Tristan quickly, so the RV Meteor, a German research vessel working in the region, was dispatched. It took several days to arrive.

Sean was carried aboard, and the ship immediately turned for Cape Town. Although his wife, Marina, was able to accompany him, there was not enough room for Kelly.

Sean died during the crossing, somewhere in the South Atlantic. Kelly has the exact coordinates tattooed on her left arm.

After her father’s funeral, Kelly returned to Tristan. But she worried that her mother felt lost without him. Marina and Sean had spent 40 years together, moving from posting to posting, and Marina had worked as a teacher at each of them. So, when a position opened at St. Mary’s School in 2025, Kelly suggested that Marina take it. She did.

For Kelly, memories of Sean are everywhere: She keeps some of his ashes in a small wooden canoe he brought from a trip to Senegal; the community named a traditional longboat “Sean B.” in his honor; her children go to school opposite the Residency where her father lived; and islanders still stop Kelly to tell her what a popular administrator he was.

“Raising a family here is amazing,” Kelly said, but she always reminds Savanna and Seren that there is also a world beyond Tristan. “There is life to experience before you decide what you want to do.”

Shane wants his children to study off the island if they choose to, but he is just as intent on teaching them to splice rope, plant potatoes, or catch fish from the beach — skills they can fall back on if they decide to stay.

item.title: Israel’s High-Stakes Election: What to Know
item.description:
Israelis are heading to the polls on Tuesday to vote in what many say could be one of the most consequential elections in the country’s 78-year history.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, the country’s longest-serving leader, his party and his governing coalition have been locked in a tight contest in the country’s first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led assault that ignited Israel’s devastating war in Gaza.

Every party creates a ranked list of its candidates, and voters choose a party or slate. The leader of the party with the most votes could become the country’s next prime minister — though it is not automatic — if that candidate can form a government, but the parliamentary system is complicated and involves extensive negotiations.

Here’s what to know.

Election Day is a public holiday in Israel, with schools, government offices and many public services closed. In most of the country, polls are scheduled to open at 7 a.m. local time and close at 10 p.m., with hours slightly reduced in some small communities, hospitals and prisons.

Voters are assigned to a polling station near their registered residence and may vote only at that location. There are exceptions for soldiers, people with limited mobility and prisoners, among others.

All Israeli citizens 18 or older who are registered to vote may do so with a valid identification, such as a passport, driver’s license or Israeli identification card. Israel’s Arab citizens, who make up about 20 percent of the population, could play a significant role in the vote, depending on turnout.

Unlike many democracies, Israel does not have a postal or proxy voting system, and most citizens cannot cast an absentee vote from abroad.

Israel’s electoral system uses nationwide proportional representation. Elections to the Knesset, Israel’s 120-seat Parliament, are held at least every four years, though they can happen more often. In 2022, Israeli elections were held for the fifth time in three years after the Knesset dissolved itself.

Israelis cast a single ballot for a list of candidates affiliated with a party. A party receives a number of seats proportional to the national vote it got. To gain a place in Parliament, however, a party or must receive at least 3.25 percent of the valid votes. About 10 parties are expected to clear that electoral threshold.

Official election results are expected by Nov. 4.

No single party has ever won a majority of votes, which means parties must form factions and party leaders try to forge a governing coalition of at least 61 lawmakers.

Within seven days of the official election results being announced, Israel’s president, who plays a mostly symbolic role, meets with elected representatives of the parliamentary factions.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will assign a member of the Knesset — usually the leader of the party or faction that has won the most seats — to form a government. That candidate then has 28 days to negotiate with other factions and forge alliances to form a government, which must be approved by the Knesset in a vote of confidence. That person can request a 14-day extension to the deadline.

If that effort fails, the president can select another candidate who also has 28 days to try to form a government. If that second attempt fails, a majority of Knesset members can ask the president to have a third candidate try. That person would be granted 14 days to form a government, and if that failed, new elections would be announced

If a candidate who has been selected to form a government can propose one, along with a policy agenda, and their proposal wins a plurality of votes in the Knesset, the government is formally invested, and that candidate becomes the prime minister. Technically, the law allows for a minority government if the relative majority supporting it is larger than the minority opposing, but governments established after elections have almost always enjoyed the confidence of a majority of Knesset members, at least 61.

Historically, it has taken about 20 to 100 days to form a government, and no government has been sworn in less than 50 days after an election, according to the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank in Israel.

Different polls in the week ahead of the election have suggested different outcomes, which is “very problematic for political scientists,” said Assaf Shapira, who heads political research at the Israel Democracy Institute, a nonpartisan think tank in Israel.

Many Israelis consider this election to be a referendum on Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership. Mr. Netanyahu and his Likud party, and their hard-right allies, are in a close race with Gadi Eisenkot, a former military chief of staff who heads the opposition coalition led by the Yashar party and has emerged as Mr. Netanyahu’s top challenger.

item.title: What to Know as Serbia Votes for a New Parliament
item.description:
Voters in Serbia choose a new Parliament on Sunday, in an election that will test whether nearly two years of student-led protests against the political establishment reflect wider public opinion or just youthful anger out of sync with the majority.

The vote pits the governing party of Aleksandar Vucic, Serbia’s dominant political figure since 2012, against a slate of candidates selected by activists in the vanguard of the protests, which began in November 2024.

The demonstrations have raged on and off since then, attracting hundreds of thousands of people in cities across the country. Some polls indicate that Mr. Vucic’s main opposition, a new political grouping called “Student List-Students Win,” could get as many votes as the governing party, or even more.

Opinion polls in Serbia, however, are notoriously unreliable, heavily biased in favor of whoever commissions them.

Still, the vote is being seen as Serbia’s most competitive in years, a pivotal moment akin to the 2000 presidential election narrowly lost by Slobodan Milosevic, Serbia’s authoritarian nationalist leader during the Balkan wars of the 1990s. Preliminary official results are expected to be released late Sunday or early Monday.

The election comes just six months after voters in neighboring Hungary rejected their longtime leader Viktor Orban, a close ally of Mr. Vucic’s who, like the Serbian leader, championed populist nationalist politics.

Serbia has the largest territory, population and economy of the seven countries that emerged from the ruins of Yugoslavia, and it is the linchpin of the region’s stability.

Since Mr. Milosevic’s fall, it has been stuck in limbo between Russia, its traditional protector with a shared Orthodox Christian faith, and the European Union, which Serbia applied to join in 2009. That process has largely stalled under Mr. Vucic, who resigned as president last month to seek the post of prime minister, which he has held twice before.

President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia has effectively endorsed Mr. Vucic, saying at a conference in early October that he hoped the Serbian leader would return as prime minister. But Russia, like the European bloc, has at times been exasperated by Serbia’s refusal to clearly pick a side. Mr. Vucic frames his policy, which he calls “two stools,” as a skillful balancing act between East and West, but others deride it as indecisive and opportunistic.

He has infuriated the European Union by refusing to impose sanctions on Russia over the war in Ukraine. But he has also angered Russia by turning a blind eye to the sale, through middlemen, of large quantities of Serbian weapons and ammunition to Ukraine.

Mocking Mr. Vucic’s mixed messaging before he stepped down as president, Maria Zakharova, the Russian foreign ministry’s spokeswoman, asked: “Is there really only one President Vucic?”

The Student List has also avoided taking clear-cut positions on foreign policy, reflecting the wide diversity of opinion in its ranks. Its candidates, nearly all political novices drawn from academia, sports, trade unions and the professions, include pro-European liberals, Russia-friendly nationalists and others in between.

It has, like Mr. Vucic, balked at insistent demands from the European bloc that Serbia join sanctions on Russia, announcing recently that it opposed doing so. But some analysts see that as a pre-election gambit to avoid alienating voters sympathetic to Russia, and many in the opposition are eager to unblock the logjam preventing entry to the European Union.

The Student List has not promised to accelerate that process, but an opposition victory would remove one important obstacle: alarm in Brussels over democratic backsliding since Mr. Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party came to power in 2012.

Whatever government is formed after the election, it will struggle to resolve the most rancorous issue poisoning Serbia’s relations with many countries in the Balkans and beyond: the status of Kosovo, which declared independence from Serbia in 2008. Mr. Vucic and many Student List candidates insist that Kosovo remains Serbian territory.

Mr. Vucic and his party, which has been rebranded for the election as Aleksandar Vucic — United Serbia, have campaigned on a twin message: nationalism and economic success. They have cast their opponents as traitors in cahoots with Croatia and Serbia’s other enemies in the 1990s, when the multiethnic state of Yugoslavia to which they had all belonged disintegrated in war.

Like Mr. Vucic, who was Mr. Milosevic’s information minister, Student List candidates have at times embraced nationalist themes. But they have struggled to shake off the “anti-Serb” label applied to their movement by a vast and often outrageously mendacious media machine controlled by the governing party.

“It is terrible what their propaganda is capable of,” said Rasa Nedeljkov, a program director at the Center for Research, Transparency and Accountability, a research group in Belgrade, the capital, that is often critical of the government. “It has absolutely no limits.”

The governing party has also boasted of its success in building new highways and attracting foreign investment from Europe as well as China, which has built large factories in Serbia and helped rescue a huge steel mill from bankruptcy.

The economy could grow this year by nearly 4 percent — far more than in most of Europe and twice the pace in Hungary, where economic troubles and widespread corruption eroded support for Mr. Orban.

The Student List, like the protest movement from which it emerged, has hammered the government over corruption, the same issue Mr. Orban’s opponents put at the center of their successful campaign.

Corruption in Serbia has grown steadily worse since Mr. Vucic first became prime minister in 2014, according to Transparency International, which last year for the first time ranked it as the most corrupt in the region.

The student-led protests began in 2024 after 16 people were killed by falling concrete at a newly renovated railway station in the city of Novi Sad. Many blamed the deaths on inspectors on the take and corrupt deals between officials and construction contractors.

The playing field is titled heavily in favor of the governing party, which controls the national electoral commission; most media outlets, including all television stations with national reach; and also state-owned companies, whose managers owe their jobs to Mr. Vucic and can easily pressure employees over how to vote.

In a report on the last election for Parliament in 2023, an arm of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe said the vote had been “technically well-administered” but “was marred by harsh rhetoric, bias in the media, pressure on public sector employees and misuse of public resources.” The governing party’s “systemic advantages” and the dominant role of then-President Vucic in a legislative election “created unjust conditions for contestants,” the report said.

The same organization reported in July that the government had since addressed some, but not its most important concerns.

The electoral commission has put the total number of registered voters at 6,450,523 — a figure that raised eyebrows, given that Serbia’s total population, including children, is only around 6.5 million. Members of the commission associated with the opposition called the number suspiciously high, but pro-Vucic members, who form a majority, prevailed.

If the race is as tight as many expect, the final result could hinge on the votes of more than 100,000 Serbian citizens who live abroad, a demographic that in many countries leans toward the opposition. In what Mr. Vucic’s opponents see as an effort to reduce overseas turnout, the electoral commission changed the rules this year and tied voting to the time in Serbia.

That means voters in Australia, which is home to a large Serbian diaspora, will have to vote at night. The window for casting ballots in Chicago, another place with a large Serbian community, will open at 1 a.m.

Milan Protic, a former Serbian ambassador to Washington, said Mr. Vucic was “trying to play every card he has left because, for the first time, he is not in full control.” He added: “Maybe, just maybe, his time is up.”

Alisa Dogramadzieva contributed reporting.

item.title: Saudi Arabia Reopens Riyadh Airport After Weeks of Houthi Attacks
item.description:
The authorities in Saudi Arabia reopened an international airport in the capital on Sunday after a spate of deadly attacks, even as the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen vowed to keep striking the facility.

King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, the capital, said on Saturday night that flights would resume on Sunday. In a statement, it advised travelers to “verify the status of their bookings and flights before heading to the airport.”

The airport had been closed to the public since Oct. 10, when a cruise missile launched by the Houthis struck a passenger terminal, killing at least 13 people and injuring more than 300. The militia, based in northern Yemen, has launched at least three other deadly strikes on the airport this month — part of its near-daily attacks on Riyadh.

On Sunday morning, residents of the capital received an emergency alert warning of an incoming “aerial threat” and some reported hearing several loud booms. The Saudi authorities said soon after that they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh.

A Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, had renewed a warning to airlines and travelers after the airport issued its statement about reopening, saying to avoid using the airport “because it is a military target.” The Saudi government, he said, would “bear responsibility for the consequences” of reopening it.

The Saudi authorities did not immediately respond to questions about how they had assessed it was safe to reopen the airport, or if they had put in place additional air defenses.

After four years of relative peace, the Houthis and the Saudis resumed attacking each other earlier this month amid the broader U.S.-Israeli war with Iran, the Houthis’ primary backer.

The Houthis describe their attacks as retaliation for deadly Saudi airstrikes in Yemen, including many that have killed and injured civilians.

On Saturday, Mr. Saree claimed in a statement that the militia had carried out an operation against the airport, among other attacks around the country, without specifying when.

The Saudi authorities have not said whether the airport was targeted this weekend. The Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen, which is fighting the Houthis, said it had intercepted missiles and drones heading toward Riyadh on Friday, Saturday and Sunday.

It was not immediately clear how many flights were departing from or landing in Riyadh airport on Sunday, or whether airlines other than Saudi state-owned carriers would opt to resume flights.

Flightradar24, a flight tracking website, showed that a Saudi Arabian Airlines plane flying from Jeddah had landed in Riyadh on Sunday afternoon. It also showed that dozens of flights to and from Riyadh had been canceled.

In recent weeks, fighting has reignited inside Yemen between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia.

A Saudi-led bombing campaign launched against the Houthis a decade ago aimed to rout the militia and restore the government. It lasted for years and precipitated one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, contributing to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people in Yemen from violence, hunger and disease.

A truce in 2022 brought a fragile peace to the country and left the Houthis in control of northern Yemen.

Tensions began to rise again after the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February, sparking a regional war. In July, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking the international airport in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in order to prevent an Iranian plane from landing.

The militia declared a blockade on Saudi oil exports in the Red Sea, and both sides began to launch a series of escalating attacks. After a full-blown war reignited earlier this month, the militia turned its focus to Saudi airports, threatening to turn them into a “theater of military operations.”

In doing so, they have hit at the heart of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s ambitions to transform the kingdom from an insular, oil-dependent nation into a global hub for business and tourism.

The prince, Saudi Arabia’s de facto ruler, recently launched a new international airline with its hub in Riyadh. His annual investment summit typically draws billionaires, executives and officials from around the world to Riyadh and was set to begin on Monday. However, it was postponed at the last minute until 2027.

The United States ordered all “non-emergency government employees and their family members” to leave Saudi Arabia, a State Department spokesman, Tommy Pigott, said on social media last week.

Despite the Houthi threats, Saudi officials have sought to maintain a sense of normalcy. The authorities kept Riyadh airport open after two deadly attacks, closing it only after the mass casualty event on Oct. 10.

In the face of the attacks, Saudi Arabia has been seeking support from allies. Last week, Britain said that it would send fighter jets to help defend Saudi cities and critical infrastructure from the Houthis.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.
